REPORTED MOVEMENT TO BOLIVIA On the Orders of the Day:

I would like to ask if the government are aware that a large number of Alberta farmers who were under contract to purchase land from the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, finding themselves unable to meet their payments, made proposals to that company which were rejected, and that these farmers are now negotiating with the Bolivian government with a view to purchasing land in Bolivia, and intend, or are even now making preparations, to move out as a colony of settlers to that country. If the government has heard of this, I would like to know if any action has been taken; whether the Canadian Pacific Railway have been approached on the matter; and whether there is any hope of holding these, farmers in Canada.

speechtext: What list?

A list of articles which enter into the manufacture of different articles in this section which we struck out.
I may say that the only sections that were struck out in committee, so far as I know, and I was here all the time, were the first three. The general resolution was not put.
That is my understanding.

My hon. friend was to check the list. I have been handed this list which I suppose is the correct one.
I do not wTant to delay my hon. friend by going over it all. Perhaps the committee would allow me to put it on Hansard.
No. The situation yesterday, as I recall it, was that my hon. friend submitted a list of articles which he claimed entered into the production-

I asked if it did;
I said I did not know.

-of these materials. I was aware of this list before, I knew it had been freely circulated, an intimation was made in the public press, that the tariff concessions affected all these items. I am sure my hon. friend will not expect me to explain in detail the extent to which these different items do enter into the production of these articles affected by the tariff. What I did was to supply my hon. friend with a comparison of the rates of duty-the old rates of duty under the general tariff and the new rates-and the percentage of these that will go into the items affected by the tariff. I make no commitments, but I say if my hon. friend will refer to the bottom of the memorandum I have given him he will find a reservation there, that articles for resale, in condition as imported would be subject to the usual rates applicable to such articles, and are not admissible under tariff item 445a.
Certainly.
That means that when the manufacturer goes to the customs claiming admission for these he must establish to the satisfaction of the officers that the articles will enter into the cost of production.
I did not expect my hon. friend to be able to give us the percentages that he referred to.
Oh no.

That would mean
a great deal of study and a good deal of delay. But I want to find out if these are articles that enter into the manufacture, that is what I was trying to find out; and I supposed my hon. friend's list would show that these articles do enter into the manufacture of these goods. That is all.

I will admit at once that looking over the list casually I should say a good many of the articles enter into the manufacture but to what extent or percentage I would not undertake to say. It might be that a very trifling part of these items would enter into the construction of an implement, or product, affected by the reductions in the tariff.

I am not asking for percentages, and I do not want to delay my hon. friend. I just want to know whether these articles enter into the manufacture and to what extent they are used. My hon. friend has prepared a list here himself which reads:
The following articles when imported by manufacturers of goods enumerated in tariff items 445, 440, 446b, 447b, 448 and 591 for use only in the manufacture of such goods enumerated in said items are rated as below.
Then we have the list. I suppose this list prepared by my hon. friend is correct.
It is correct.
Then, instead of asking my hon. friend to read his list, in order to facilitate the work of the committee I am quite content it should be handed to Hansard.

Let me clear this up with my hon. friend now. I want to be perfectly frank with him. This was checked out from a list that circulated freely in the public press and was supplied, I understand, by the Manufacturers' Association. It is the Manufacturers' Association that make the statement that these different items are affected by the reduction in the tariff, I am not prepared to guarantee that all that is put out there is correct. I would say in a general way that many of these items do go into the manufacture of such articles as are affected by the tariff, but I would not certify that they all go in.

I notice "Goggles" here.
If goggles go in, paint might as well go too.

in the construction of agricultural implements?
If my hon. friend says they do not that is all I want to get.	*
I say they do not.

Very well, what else besides brooms? Surely my hon. friend takes his budget proposals a little more seriously than to laugh. We are dealing with tariff items and we want to know what items are affected. I have given a list to my hon. friend for the purpose of being checked over to see whether it contains correctly the items affected. Now he tells me that in one case it is not correct-brooms. Very well, take that out; is there anything else that is not correct?

I am not going to check the
list.

Well, I just
point out, Mr. Chairman, the way this House is legislating upon this question. The minister does not know what articles he is dealing vith, or what articles are affected by these changes.
file CHAIRMAN: (Mr. Marcil, Bonaven-;ure):	Shall the item carry?

What is the
minister going to do about my suggestion of putting the list on Hansard? It is his list.

I have no objection to my
hon. friend putting the list on Hansard, with this reservation-that I do not admit they all go into the production.
There is apparently one thing we can agree on, that is that my hon. friend does not know what is affected.
I would not admit that.

Until this moment I have not had an opportunity of examining this list, but if I understand it aright it is a list prepared by somebody of articles which probably or possibly enter into the manufacture of agricultural implements and by reason thereof the present duties will be reduced. I notice on the list the old rate and the new rate of duty. In the riding which I have the honour to represent while we are not to a very large extent engaged in the manufacture of agricultural implements as such, there are a great many items on this list which are manufactured there. I take the first item, wagon springs. Apparently the old rate of duty is 17i per cent. The new rate according tc this list is 6 per cent. Will the minister tell me whether in the case of wagon springs- which are made largely in Guelph-the"reduction will be from 17J to 6 per cent?

On springs going into a
vjagon-that is affected by this tariff, yes.

That is, a farm wagon,
The next item is coil springs, which are also made in my city, and which are used to some extent in various kinds of agricultural machinery. The present duty on coil springs is 30 per cent, which under the new arrangement will be reduced to 6 per cent. Do I understand that the duty on all coil springs that go into agricultural implements of any kind will now be reduced from 30 per cent to 6 per cent?

If they go into the agricultural implement that is affected by this, yes. Let me point out to my hon. friend that the manufacturer of coil springs will also have some concessions by way of reduction of duty )n his raw material.

That is just what I
wanted to ask. If the manufacturer makes coil springs which ultimately go into agricultural implements, what provision is made for him; does he get his raw material in free?

No. If it is established that
he is at a disadvantage, the government will try to put him in a reasonable position. Let me clear this up with my hon. friend at once. \V hen the tariff was first announced hon. gentlemen opposite, in the House and through their press, said that the agricultural implement industry of this country was ruined, that the government were practically putting it out of business. But shortly afterwards the manufacturers of agricultural implements issued a statement saying they were able to carry on, and it was established, I think, by a

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
supporter of my hon. friend's, that these manufacturers were almost in as good a position as they were before; indeed there were some hon. gentlemen who reversed their position later on and declared the manufacturers of agricultural implements were even in a better position than they had been before; but statements were then made in this House and in the press that the steel industry was to be ruined by the action of the government. But the same newspapers which announced that our steel industries were closing down their furnaces because of the action of the government, printed in their financial pages announcements from the managers of these industries that they had orders enough to keep them going until September. No later than yesterday in the Montreal Star-and no one will contend that this paper is over zealous in supporting the government-in the financial column -not in the political column, be k noted-Mr. Hobson, who is a recognized leader in the steel industry of Canada, gave out a statement which I will read for the benefit of my hon. friend. This is the announcement :
Expects steel business to pick up a little.
Toronto May 22.-(Star Special).-
The rumour that Steel Company of Canada had decided to curtail operations was definitely denied this morning by President Robert Hobson, of that company, who, while he would not say that the outlook was particularly bright', was distinctly optimistic as to the immediate outlook, saying that operations were continuing at a fair rate, approximately 70 per cent capacity.
"The outlook is regarded with a little more confidence generally." said Mr. Hobson, who added that he could see indications that business might pick up a little rather than the reverse.
Mr. Hobson further stated that a second furnace would be blown in during the course of the next three or four weeks, and set at rest various rumours by explaining the reason for the temporary shutdown. The furnace, he said, had been put in in 1896 and its shell had been worn almost completely through. It had been closed to permit the construction of a new shell. This work was well under way and would be completed within the next three weeks and the blast put into operation again.
So I am inclined to take Mr. Hobson as an authority on the steel industry of Canada rather than my hon. friend opposite. This government has no intention of ruining any Canadian industries. We want and expect our industries, as a result of the budget, to do more business and employ more hands than ever before.	'

After his speech the minister perhaps will turn for a. moment to the question I asked him:	Will the manufacturers of wagon springs and of coil springs be entitled to get in their raw material under any better rate in future than they
have in the past? I understood my hon. friend to say that they would have some relief. I did not find it in his budget speech, nor do I find it in his schedules. I wish he would point out to me where it is.

I say frankly to my hon. friend, realizing fully the responsibility of the statement, that if it can be established that industries manufacturing these different parts are adversely affected by the tariff to a degree that they require consideration, the government will be prepared to give them fair consideration.

Does the minister make that statement under authority? He cannot alter the tariff, as he knows, after parliament has prorogued. Does he propose bringing in some legislation this session empowering him to make these changes? Or under what authority does he intend to act?
My hon. friends will have to accept my statement, as I hope the manufacturers will.
Is there any foundation for the statement?
There is sincerity in it.

That may be the pious wish of the minister himself. If he brings in legislation giving him the power, that would be foundation enough. He knows that once the tariff act is passed, it is final until the House meets again. Will there be any chance, say next autumn or next winter before the House meets, of the manufacturers of steel wagon springs and of coil springs obtaining relief in respect of their raw materials where their springs go into faftn *wagons and agricultural implements? The minister said they might rest assured that they would be taken care of, or words to that effect. I wish he would give me some assurance on which they can do business.
Mr. FORIvE: Is the item fuel oil correct? It is put at lOOi per cent.
It is a typewriting error; it should be one-half cent.

I take another item in which my constituency is particularly interested-pipe.	This list simply has the
item "pipe". As the minister knows, perhaps, there is a large industry in Guelph making iron pipe. Pipe is now marked on this list 30 per cent, and the proposed reduction will put it down to 6 per cent. Do I understand

If it goes into the manufacture of an article that only bears 6 per cent duty.

Is the same thing correct in regard to belt pulleys? They are made in the city of Guelph too. The reduction in this case is from 271 to 6 per cent. Does the minister contemplate, in regard to the pipe industry or the manufacture of belt pulleys, that any advantage will be given to these manufacturers to compensate them for the reduction which they must now face where their goods enter into the manufacture of agricultural implements? Can the minister give me any assurance? I want it for the purpose of passing it on to the manufacturers of whom I speak. If he can, it will be gratefully received in the city of Guelph where these things are made.

Careful consideration will have to be given as to what percentage of the output of an industry is affected by the tariff changes. If an industry is enjoying twenty, twenty-five or thirty per cent protection on ninety per cent of its products and the other ten per cent is affected by these changes, 1 am not so sure that it would be possible to make out a case. But we will look into the matter very carefully.

Have only two of these lists been prepared? What is the idea of supplying two members of the House with a list which the rest of the House does not have if we are expected to consider these it^ms with any intelligence?

We are at item No. 12A, "sausage
skins or casings, cleaned," and all this discussion does not refer to this item at all.

I provided those lists as a
matter of courtesy to the hon. member who was leading the opposition this afternoon and the hon. member who was leading the Progressives. I do not place so much importance upon the list as my hon. friends seem to do, as it was a list that was issued and widely circulated by the Manufacturers' Association, in an attempt to convince the people that we were ruining the country. May I point this out again?-that as regards many of these items, the great percentage of production of an industry is affected very slightly. I should like to appeal to the judgment of my hon. friend (Mr. Caldwell), who knows something 
about farming, or potato growing anyway, if I cannot appeal to the genial member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton); will he tell me to what extent disinfectants will enter into the manufacture of agricultural implements? -to what extent will tungsten lamps enter into the manufacture of agricultural implements?-to what extent will electrical equipment enter into their manufacture? There are three items that just come to my attention. It is sufficient, I think, to mention those items to show, to say the least, that this list is considerably padded.

I almost thought for
the moment that we were considering the items on thig list. If that is not what we are considering as items under the tariff, possibly k is not very relevant, and therefore my objection has been removed. So far as I can gather from this list, it is about on a par with the claim made by the manufacturers as regards the whole tariff. Much of the literature circulated by them is an attempt to becloud the issue entirely.

The reason why this list is here is because, instead of wasting the time of the committee in an endeavour to get information from the minister when he did not have it, I handed in a list and he said that he would check it. If you will look at Hansard at page 2422, the minister says:
I will be quite content to take the list and have the customs authorities who are to administer the act, look carefully into it and check it over.
I then said:
I will put it on Hansard, and then the minister can have it cheeked. My instructions are that these are only some of the things.
What I wanted to get at was the truth, that is all. The minister was to have the list checked and was to let us know the result. I do not know what position he wants to take to-day, whether he is going to say that what he said before is not to be acted upon; but I can assure him that he will not make much progress taking that stand.

I can see now that when
my hon. friend spoke of "checking," he had one thing in mind and I had another. I understood him to mean that we would check the difference in the duty if these items went into the manufacture of agricultural implements.
No.

I say frankly to my hon.
friend that at this stage of the legislation I would not undertake to find out what goods

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
enter into the manufacture of articles affected by this legislation; but that will be carefully checked, and a manufacturer will have to establish to the satisfaction of the Department of Customs and Excise that an item goes in to the manufacture of agricultural implements before he will have consideration for rebates.

My hon. friend
is entirely at another point and there was no room for any misunderstanding. If my hon. friend will look at page 2421 of Hansard, when I W3s picking out some of these items and asking whether my hon. friend knew whether they were affected or not, my hon. friend admitted that some of them were. My hon. friend said:
We will admit they are going in as farm machinery.
That is, these items that I was referring to.
I said:
I do not want to be unfair to my hon. friend. If he does not know, it is unfair for me to go on establishing facts, because he may be stating something which is not correct. I only want the truth, and I want to know what we are legislating about.
There was no question of tariff at all. It was a question of the items, whether an article was or was not affected. I continued:
I suggest to my hon. friend that he should bring down a list of all the articles entering into the manufacture of articles which will be covered by these reductions. He will have it right then.
We had some more discussion and I handed that list to my hon. friend to be checked. I cannot understand why there is any room for a difference of opinion as to what Hansard said.

I do not dispute what Hansard says, but I had in mind that the request was to check the rate of duty. Had I thought that my hon. friend wanted me to send out to the different manufacturers and inquire from them to what extent these various items would enter into their industry, I would have at once made it clear to him that I did not propose to do that. I do not propose to do it now.

My hon. friend
would be quite right if he says: "To what extent?" I did not ask that. I asked only if these items entered into manufacture of farm machinery. The situation resolved itself into this, that the government have brought in these resolutions without knowing what articles they are affecting, and although it is now six weeks since the budget proposals were brought down, the government even today do not know what they are doing and will not take the trouble to find out.

It would be an utter impossibility for the government at this time to bring down every article that will enter into the manufacture of all kinds of implements.
I think the hon. member who is leading the opposition is asking an impossibility. I may be wrong, but I do not see how this is possible.

Yes, the hon.
member is quite wrong. It is an easy matter.

I am much obliged to the
hon. member for the kindly advice he always hands out to me when I am on my feet, but I have an opinion of my own, anyway.

The list has only come
to my attention to-day. It is very interesting to me and it will be very interesting to the riding which I have the honour to represent.

My hon. friend says that this list has only come to his attention to-day. He told us a moment ago that he represents a constituency that is interested largely in the manufacture- of these products that enter into the manufacure of farm machinery. How does he explain that he has heard of this list only to-day? Are his constituents not interested in it?

I did not see this list
until five minutes ago when I noticed it o* the desk of my hon. friend (Sir Henry Drayton) who is sitting next to me. Let me at once direct the
attention of my hon. friend to item 1027, which we shall reach once we get this one out of the way. Item 1027 reads:	'
Materials, when used by manufacturers of malleable iron castings or steel shafting for use exclusively in the manufacture of such articles for use in the manufacture of goods enumerated in tariff items 445, 446, 446b. 447b. 448 and 591.
In that case there is an 80 per cent rebate on the duty.

To what extent is the article mentioned in item 12a imported?
We have not reached that item yet. I will give the information when we come to it.

The hon. member for
South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) makes a distinctly sectional plea; he speaks for the people of Guelph, whom he particularly represents. Well, I want to say a word or two for the people I represent. My hon. friend says that the people he represents will be injured if any of the privileges they have hitherto enjoyed under a protective tariff or under a high tariff are taken away. I claim, Sir, that the people I represent have been injured for many years by the tariff and will still be injured by the proposed tariff, but the injury will be less. They have to go out in the open world and find a market wherever they can for the goods they produce, and they have been obliged by the tariff to take the money they get for their goods, go to Ontario and Quebec and purchase the things they need at prices which are enhanced by the tariff. It is the most inequitable legislation that could be put on the statute books. The people I
represent cannot under any possible conditions receive benefit from any tariff or any protective tariff that can be introduced. My hon. friend says that the people of Guelph particularly are receiving advantage from the customs tariff that has been in operation. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler) makes the same claim, as do the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler), the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Raymond), and several others. Taking these statements at their face value, I submit that if the people living in the neighbourhood of those cities are benefited by the customs duties, in the name of fair play they should pay for those advantages. Let them provide this payment in any way they wish-by bounties; that would be a simple way of doing it.
A benevolent way.

A fair way. I would have no objection to that, but I protest as strongly as I can against the people I represent being compelled to pay for the advantages that the people living in Guelph and in the neighbourhood of Guelph enjoy. It cannot be called a "national" policy. I want to bring that view to the attention of my hon. friend, who, I believe, is a fair man and wants to be an honest and a just man. I ask him to consider the people I represent as well as those he represents, and to give us all fair play.
Make an average.
Yes, make an average.

What do you mean by an
average?

I mean we should have
an average of justice in this country.
An average of justice,-that is a new one.

It is certainly new in
this country.
An average of fair play.
We ought to have fair play, not an average of fair play. Fair play is a definite thing. The term "average fair play" is absurd.
The position taken by the hon. member for North Waterloo in regard to the protective tariff is unjust as well as absurd.

I suppose it is "average
injustice," is it?

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff

My hon. friend can speak
in this committee whenever he wishes. I am making a statement now, and I am sure that I make it to men who recognize justice and fair play. I think, too, that I have some backing in what I say.

In regard to the item to
which the minister called my attention- 1027, materials when used by manufacturers of malleable iron castings-do those materials include fuel coal or steam coal?
No.

The minister
does not know whether these new tariff changes may become necessary or whether he is going to make exemptions or modifications under section 286 of the Customs Act, but if he is not going to do it that way, how is he going to do it?

It can be done under section
286 of the Customs Act if it is found necessary.

So the present idea is that any injustices that develop, and which the minister would not be guilty of if he knew what he was doing, are to be cured under section 286 of the Customs Act. What are the principles under which the government will act in correcting those injustices? Take for example the case he himself gives, where there is but a small percentage used of a firm's output affected by these tariff reductions. What percentage, in my hon. friend's view, would have to be shown before the government would interfere and aid? In the case of the small percentage he mentioned he seemed to think that nothing ought to be done. Just where would he consider action necessary under section 286?

That is a very fair question. My hon. friend has had some experience: He travelled, I think, from Halifax to Vancouver taking evidence as to revision of the tariff. I am not sure that he ever went much further than that, but he had the evidence and he probably has very definite ideas as to what should be done. Generally speaking, I think the question of where tariff protection should be afforded should be very carefully gone into. I. think the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) made it clear in his speech on the budget that the government proposed to go very carefully into the conditions throughout Canada during the year. One item that might be very carefully looked into, for instance, in industries enjoying tariff protection would be the 
amount of watered stock they had. I think the people of Canada have a right to know whether these industries are paying dividends on watered stock or not. There are many other considerations affecting industries that my hon. friend knows must be taken into account.
I do not like to delay the passing of my own resolutions, nor to prolong this debate, which in the House continued from the 10th of April up to the 15th of May, but I would like again to remind my hon. friends opposite that they have not kept one principle steadily in view in the consideration of these tariff changes. I repeat again that in the early period we were said to be destroying the agricultural implement industry in this country; then we were destroying the steel industry. Mr. Chairman, I want to say at the outset of my remarks that this subject is not a theory for me, it affects the business in which I have been engaged for about 35 years, it affects my life's work, and anything I say will refer not only to the business in which I am particularly interested, but it will also be typical of other iron and steel manufacturing concerns. Of course, we have to bear in mind that the amount of damage done to any industry is in direct proportion to the amount of the output that will be affected by these tariff items. I have had no communication with other makers of this material, and know nothing about what they have in mind, and what I have to say will simply be based on what I know of the business myself. It has been suggested that these appeals have been sectional in their character, but my appeal will be applicable wherever the business of making agricultural implements is carried on and wherever the supplies of raw materials for those implements are made.

I should like to say a few words about the treatment of the iron and steel industry during the last few years. Iron and steel bars under the tariff of 1907 were subject to a tariff levy of $7 per ton in the genera! tariff, $6 per ton in the intermediate and $4.25 per ton in the British preferential. On account of the lowering of tariffs on agricultural implements, the duty on materials, particularly iron and steel, of which I am speaking now, used in their manufacture, has been gradually reduced, thus making the position of the industry gradually worse. In the 1907 tariff, item No. 1002 provides for a drawback of 99 per cent of the duty paid on iron and steel bars entering into the manufacture of binders and mowers. In 1919, another reduction was made in agricultural implement duties, and articles entering into the manufacture of cultivators, ploughs, engines, threshers, tractors, fruit-grading machines, hay loaders and wagons were all made subject to a 30 per cent drawback of duty. In 1922, by item No. 1026, a drawback was provided for of 40 per cent of the duty paid on materials entering into cultivators, ploughs, threshing machines, fruit and vegetable-grading machines, hay loaders, rollers and milking machines. In 1922, under item No. 1027, a drawback was provided for of 30 per cent of the duty on materials entering into the manufacture of portable engines, street and road rollers, and farm wagons. In the same year, item No. 1028 provided for a drawback of 99 per cent of the duty paid on materials entering into gas tractors not over $1,400 in value. In 1923, item No. 1.036 provided for a drawback of duty of 30 per cent on materials entering into the manufacture of stumping machines. Those are about all the reductions that have been made in the iron and steel duties until the present budget. A considerable quantity of fire brick is used in the manufacture of this material and this fire brick was free of duty until 1922. In that year fire brick was placed at 15 per cent duty, so that the industry not only lost the protective duty on the materials I have mentioned, but suffered the imposition of a 15 per cent duty on fire brick. The items now being considered obliterate the duties on rolled iron and steel entering into a long list of implements. There possibly may be some explanation as regards the different opinions that have been expressed as to the effect of this tariff. To begin with, this item included only two items in the tariff. Now, it includes six. In consideration of all those changes, the only allowance given is that proposed in another resolution which provided for again putting fire brick on the free list.

In passing, I want to call this to the attention of the minister, that because there is a cost of 6, 10 or 15 cents a bushel for threshing, it does not necessarily mean that that is the total cost, because over and above that we have to provide feed and board for ten or twelve and sometimes even as many as eighteen or twenty men. So the cost of 6, 10, or 15 cents a bushel does not represent the actual cost to the farmer. When the established farmer sees the necessity, he is obliged to secure the smaller outfit which he and a couple of hired men whom he engages in the harvest can handle completely, having his wagons there, and it is only a matter of justice that this government should now make provision for the size of separator that would correspond well with the tractor that is now let in under the $1,400 valuation, making a cheaper unit for the individual. Mr, CALDWELL: I think I can help the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) somewhat in this matter. The New York authorities had an investigation as to the growing of potatoes in Canada and the United States, and they found to their surprise that potatoes could be grown much cheaper in Canada than in the United States. This is how they arrived at that. I pointed out yesterday-and the statement cannot be refuted-that at that time we were paying ten dollars a ton more for fertilizer than in Maine just opposite to us where the test was made. As we use a ton to the acre, that is quite an item before you begin to plant. Our machinery also costs us more; but the way they figured that it costs more to grow potatoes in Maine than in New Brunswick is that they value land at $200 an acre in Maine and $20 an acre in New Brunswick, and they take into consideration interest on the investment. What was the' reason why land that was worth $200 in Maine was worth only $20 in New Brunswick, when it was identically the same on either side of the line? These farms extended along the border for some 25 miles on either side and yet there was this disparity in the prices of the land. The reason is simply that they can get more for their crops over in Maine. The farms in Maine yielded no more per acre; the land was no more fertile, and from this standpoint there was no reason for the difference in the respective prices. Owing however, to the fact, as I showed yesterday, that they could get in Maine, for every 5,000 barrels of potatoes they produced, $4,250, more than the farmers in New Brunswick could obtain for the same crop produced on the same area, the land was certainly worth more across the line. Then again the man who planted 50 acres paid for his fertilizer, if the difference was $10 a ton-and I think I showed yesterday that in sqme cases it was $13.95 in one year- $500 less for a sufficient quantity for that 50 acres than the New Brunswick farmer would have to pay. Nothwithstanding this, it seems that by the usual process of calculation they

That is Henry Ford's now.

Can the minister tell us exactly how that is? How it works out is simply this, that no duties whatever will be paid on these stamping machines. It is an old question, and the minister is right in

pointing out the difficulties of business. It is only a tardy recognition of what we have often said. These are expensive machines, and our production here is such that I think I am within the mark in saying that most automobile companies could stamp all their bodies perhaps within six weeks; so they will just- bring the machinery in and take it out again. The disability is one of overhead. In the United States, with mass production, instead of having these stamping dies going for only a month or six weeks, they would have them going all the time. But I would have thought, Mr. Chairman, that with the present tariff protection on automobiles, which is high, the country could get a little revenue out of this operation; but apparently we are to lose it in connection with a highly protected industry.

As my hon. friend has said, these machines are used for only a few days, but this reduction will place Canadians in a position to meet competition in export markets. My hon. friend must recall that we get a revenue from other sources; the more business they do, the more the export, the more revenue we get fromf these concerns. As regards the high duty on automobiles, that has often been pointed out, and it is true; but I think this is a fair source from which to get revenue. As my hon. friend knows, automobiles are imported of a special design by people who are ready to pay a high price for them, and I do not see why they should not contribute something to the revenues of this country. It is rather difficult to differentiate in the duties on automobiles as between the lower priced and the higher priced cars.

I am glad to
see my hon. friend now thinks it is worth while to manufacture for export. Of course the whole reason for our being so extensively in that business to-day, or rather the major reason is the preference given in Great Britain. I should like to know if my hon. friend is going to make any representations whatever to the British government in connection with the McKenna duties.

No, the position I take is that we would not like the British government to dictate to us what policy we should adopt in Canada. We feel that this country has been the pioneer in the matter of preferential tariffs. My hon. friend will recall the preferential tariff that was introduced many years ago in Canada by the present Minister of Finance, and which has been increased from year to year. We do believe in this country in the idea of preferential tariff but we do

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
not like to go so far as to dictate to the Mother Country or to a sister dominion, how they should frame their tariff policy, because we recognize that if we were to do so they might some day come along and attempt to interfere with our tariff, and I am sure we would resent that.

My hon. friend quite understands that there is no dictation about the matter at all, not the slightest. What has he been doing himself in connection with Australia? He is not giving Australia a preference right through. No he is trying to get some mutual understanding under which Canadian commerce will thrive and under which Australian commerce will thrive. I am asking him whether he has done in connection with Great Britain just what he is doing in connection with Australia, that is all. I am not asking him to interfere or to coerce, or do anything like that; the mere suggestion is ridiculous.

I do not know that I quite
follow my hon. friend. Does he mean that we should say to the British government "Unless you will give us a preference we will withdraw the present preference?"

Mutuality is the whole underlying idea of preferences. The preference was given in the hope that it would be followed; my hon. friend knows that perfectly well. It is his own policy but in the case of Australia he is waiting until he gets more advantage for the Canadian trader in the Australian market. Why not pursue the same policy in regard to Great Britain? My hon. friend is not consistent. He does one thing in connection with Australia, and another thing in the case of the Mother Country.

I think we should have a little further explanation as to why one industry was picked out for special exemption in connection with expensive machinery which cannot be used all the time. That is a condition which is not confined to automobiles at all. There are lots of machines in other businesses, as my hon. friend well knows, that are not used in Canada more than a fraction of the time. They are used in rhe United States owing to the mass production there. Here we have a direct admission from the government of what we have always said in connection with this mass production, and we have that admission in connnection with only one activity. That activity I think I can fairly and safely say is 158
the one which ought to be able to stand up best as being perhaps the most highly protected. Now, why does my hon. friend pick this industry out and leave all the others?

I think the ex-Minister of Finance has propounded a very proper question to the minister at this time. Surely he did not need to single out the automobile industry for free dies. He says that the automobile people probably use these machines for only six weeks in the year. Now, the farmer uses his binder about ten days in the year, but he is not singled out for a free binder on that account. I would have no objection whatever to these dies being placed on the free list if the Acting Minister of Finance had done his duty and given us a little reduction in the duty on automobiles. If we have one example in Canada of protection gone mad I think it is in connection with the duty on automobiles. Including additions to plant, and equipment, and dividends paid, the Ford Company of Canada have taken out of the pockets of the people of Canada, something like $30,000,000 in addition to the wages and everything else that they have paid, and it would be really interesting to know to just what extent Canadians have taxed themselves lo establish the automobile industry in this country. According to a publication which I have here, issued by the Toronto Board of Trade, the percentage of the capital invested in the automobile industry in Canada, which is owned in the United States, is 77.7 per cent. That is, we are taxing ourselves to the extent of 35 per cent for the benefit of some American millionaires. I should like to take this opportunity of protesting because the minister has brought down his budget without offering us any reduction whatever on automobiles.

The effect then, is that in connection with the tariff revision my hon. friend is making he is rebating to the manufacturers 99 per cent of all duties already paid on goods on hand.

On goods entering into the
manufacture, as of that date.

That is the
date upon which the new tariff comes into effect. That was also tabled on the 10th of April, was it not?
Yes, this was done to enable the industries at once to reduce the price to the Canadian farmer, putting them on a par with their foreign competitors.

It occurs to me that
this possibly goes further than the minister intended. It does not say "materials they have on hand", but all materials imported prior to the 11th of April, 1924. I am not sure that under that the manufacturers would not have a claim for rebate on all materials they had imported up to April 1924.

I think it would be safe to
add "and on hand".
You could say "imported prior to the 11th day of April, 1924, and on hand at that date."
It says "materials entering into the cost of goods imported before the first day of July, 1927." I think that covers it.
I think not.

Then clause 5 says:
Resolved, that any enactment founded on the foregoing resolutions shall be deemed to have come into force on the eleventh day of April, one thousand nine hundred and twenty-four, and to have applied to all goods mentioned in the foregoing resolutions imported or taken out of warehouse for consumption on and after that day, and to have applied to goods previously imported for which no entry for consumption was made before that day.
I think it is all right as it stands.

I think I am right
still, but if the minister is satisfied I suppose I ought to be.

What is the
significance of the further limitation, "When entering into the cost of goods enumerated in tariff items 445, 446, 446b, 447b, 448 and 591, before the first day of July 1927?"

They might have goods on
hand that they could not wipe out within a month or six months or a year, and we are giving them this time to use up their raw material.

I am not clear on this
yet. If they are to be given a rebate on all materials they have on hand prior to the 11th day of April, 1924, why should there be any further time extension to let them work it off? It does not matter what they do with it if they get the rebate.
We only give them the rebate after they have worked it up. This is to prevent them from selling it to somebody else.

Item agreed to.
Customs tariff-1027. Materials, subject' to drawback when used by manufacturers of malleable iron castings or steel shafting for use exclusively in the manufacture of such articles for use in the manufacture of goods enumerated in tariff items 445, 446, 446b, 447b, 448 and 591-payable as drawback, 80 per cent.
This is a concession to the manufacturers of malleable castings and steel shafting.
That takes the place of the 40 per cent?
Yes.

Item agreed to.
Customs tariff-1031. Artificial silk tops and waste or artificial fibre silk, artificial silk yarns or filaments enumerated in tariff items 583a and 583aa, subject to drawback when further manufactured before the first day of January, 1925-payable as drawback, 60 per cent.

What is the
idea of this? I did not notice it before, but I suppose this is because we have not yet got the artificial silk mill running.
Yes.

If that is the
reason, why is there not a greater drawback than 60 per cent? That is simply penalizing everyone doing business in Canada to the extent of 40 per cent.

I really could not answer
my hon. friend. I was not following this last session when it was put through, but this is simply extending the enactment of last year.
Sir	HENRY DRAYTON:	And it was
strenuously objected to last year, but we were told that the mill would soon be running and we need not bother about it. There is a direct handicap on Canadian progress to the extent of 40 per cent on every bit of artificial silk they use, and it is used-I forget in just what proportions-in connection with every

Ways and Means-Drawbacks
bit of botany yarn they turn out. It is simply putting a premium on the American product as against the Canadian product to the extent of 40 per cent. This is only for a year, so why not make it free for one year, or why not give them 99 per cent drawback for the year? The knitting concerns have hard enough times as it is without discriminating in this way against Canadian industry.

I understand the Finance
Minister had a conference with all interested, and that they7 were satisfied with this arrangement last year.
I can assure my hon. friend they were not.

I have put this in at the
request of representatives of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, who told me of some difficulties they have had in getting the machinery forwarded to get this mill running.

It would be a
perfect outrage not to put that in. I want to put the case to my hon. friend. This material was on the free list, as I recollect it, and Mr. Russell will know if I am wrong -I have not my papers here-

Part of it was on the free
list.

I mean this
artificial silk stuff. It was used for the purposes of manufacturing, and it was on the free list or there was a drawback of 99 per cent. Now last year we had a new infant industry started, and that infant industry was artificial silk, and in order to get this artificial silk industry going we had a whole list of protective duties introduced by the Minister of Finance, ranging as I recollect it from 15 to 37J per cent. It was pointed out in connection with that matter that this artificial silk formed the raw material in the manufacture of botany yarns and some other yarns, and so we were to have a drawback in connection with all these duties until that mill was running. It is a very small thing so why not make it 99 per cent?

I would not like to lose that
revenue.

What revenue
would be lost? It is not a fraction of the revenue that my hon. friend is handing tonight to the American producers. The only difference is that a Canadian would be getting the benefit.
What drawback do you suggest?
Ninety-nine per cent until this mill is started. It does not amount to anything.

There may be some goods o.
hand. Why not compromise and make it 8k per cent?
Very well.

I move that 80 per cent be
substituted for 60 per cent, payable as drawback.

Amendment agreed to.
Item as amended agreed to.
Customs tariff-1036. Bar iron or steel, rolled, whether in coils or bars, one and one-eighth of an inch in diameter and over subject to drawback when used in the manufacture of goods enumerated in tariff item 410-payable as drawback, 99 per cent.

This drawback is given on
account of the rate of duty being higher on the iron and steel. The rates on chain are free, 5 and 5 per cent.
Is this iron used in the making of chain?
Yes.
Of one and one-eighth of an inch in diameter and over?
Yes.

I think there is no
chain used in Canada of that diameter. What is it for,-stumping machines?
I think it is used in the north.
My fear is that the minister is not meeting the need of this case I have lumbered and have done almost anything requiring to be done with chains and I never knew of such large chain.
I made this provision at the request of a gentleman who was manufacturing this chain at Welland, Ontario.
Can you state what the chain is used for?
That size of iron is used in anchor chain, also in chains for hauling logs out of the water at the mill.
Possibly. But there would be nothing else as large as that in the shape of chains.
Not that I know of.
It is not a large item.

Is the minister satisfied that this meets the need he wishes to make provision for?

Ways and Means-Drawbacks
Yes.
I am not objecting to the item but my opinion is that this is not going to apply to any chain unless it is anchor chain, I do not know that anchor chain is made in Canada.
I am satisfied this is all the man who is manufacturing it asked for.

Item agreed to.
Customs tariff-1036. Bar iron or steely rolled, whether in coils or bars, one and one-eighth of an inch in diameter and over; subject to drawback when used in the manufacture of goods enumerated in tariff item 410-payable as drawback, 99 per cent.
Item agreed to.
Customs tariff-1038. Materials, including all parts, subject to drawback when used in the manufacture of goods enumerated in tariff item 544a-payable as drawback, 99 per cent.
Item agreed to.
Customs tariff-1038. Materials, including all parts, subject to drawback when used in the manufacture of goods enumerated in tariff item 544a-payable as drawback, 99 per cent.

The drawback is given on account of the free machinery for the manufacture of binder twine so as to enable the manufacturers in Canada, to produce the goods in this country without being at too great a disadvantage.

Item agreed to.
Customs tariff-1039. Materials, including all parts not finished, subject to drawback when used in the manufacture of goods enumerated in tariff items 447 and 448b-payable as drawback, 30 per cent.
This is a reclassification, there is no change except that tariff item 591 "farm wagons" has been taken out and the materials may now be entered under 445a.

Item agreed to.
Customs tariff-1040. Bags, boxes and barrels, subject to drawback when imported by producers of salt, for use in covering salt produced in Canada-payable as drawback, 60 per cent.

Salt packages are free when containing salt from the United Kingdom and there is a low rate when importations are made under the general tariff. The drawback is to equalize the duty paid on packages used by the Canadian producers of salt.

Item agreed to.
Customs tariff-1041. Materials, subject to drawback when used in the manufacture of bags, boxes and barrels, when such bags, boxes and barrels are used in covering salt produced in Canada-payable as drawback, 60 per cent.

The same reasons obtain here as in the case of the previous item.
fMr. Caldwell.]
Only this applies to the machinery that is used in the manufacture of these bags, boxes and barrels.
And the materials.
Item agreed to.

I beg to move that the following be inserted after tariff item 1041:
Customs tariff-1042. Materials, including all parts, subject to drawback when entering into the cost of cyanide of potassium and cyanide of sodium-payable as drawback, 99 per cent.
Where did the request for this come from?
The article is free and so we propose to give the material going into it a rebate of 99 per cent.
Item agreed to.

I beg to move that the following be inserted after tariff item 1042:
Customs tariff-1043. Materials, including all parts, subject to drawback, which entered into the cost of goods enumerated in tariff items 445, 446, 446b, 447b, 448 and 591, on hand or in process of manufacture, in possession of the manufacturer and unsold, on the tenth day of April, 1924. Provided that drawback payable under this item is in lieu of drawback payable under any other tariff item-payable as drawback, 99 per cent.
Explain.

This is a further concession
that was made on the promise that the price of the implements in question would be reduced to the Canadian farmer.

Yes, but we
have already got one drawback. I appreciate that my hon. friend has been doing everything he can to get them to reduce these costs. I can tell my hon. friend one thing: He is going to get a reduction all right in the price of all these things if the present movement goes on in the States in connection with the steel values which will have to come here too. I noticed' to-day, and I have no doubt my hon. friend did, in a letter published from Boston very substantial decreases. Now what is really the difference between drawback item 1026 and drawback item 1043? What is the idea?

These are the finished machines that are on hand. The other had to do with the raw material. We are taking into account the material that entered into the construction of machines that were already manufactured and ready to be shipped.

I would have
thought that the other one would have been just as good.

Ways and Means-Sales Tax
This clears the matter up for administrative purposes.

The idea, as
the minister explains it, is to cover the case of the completed goods as yet unsold.
Item agreed to.

I beg to move that the following be inserted after tariff item 1043:
Customs tariff-1044. Fire brick, subject to drawback, when imported by manufacturers of iron or steel for use exclusively in the construction or repair of a blast furnace, open hearth furnace or rolling mill furnace-payable as drawback, 99 per cent.

It is estimated the reduction
of revenue will be $75,000. It is a concession to the steel mills.

This will all
come from the States will it not?
I think so.

None of this is made
in Canada?
Practically none. Some brick is made on the Pacific coast.
There is a factory in Medicine Hat.

That was not represented to
us. We were advised that there is one at Clayburn on the Pacific coast, but that the freight did not enable the product to be sold to eastern steel men.

Amendment agreed to.
5. Resolved, That any enactment founded on the foregoing resolutions shall be deemed to have come into force on the eleventh day of April, one thousand nine hundred and twenty-four, and to have applied to all goods mentioned in the foregoing resolutions imported or taken out of warehouse for consumption on and after that day, and to have applied to goods previously imported for which no entry for consumption was made before that day.
I think that is the usual form.
Resolution agreed to.
Shall we go on with the sales tax? I thought we might run on till ten o'clock, but it is whatever my hon. friend says.

I notice we
have a great many vacant seats, but perhaps we could go on till ten o'clock. I might be able to facilitate my hon. friend by giving him information on the sales tax which he will have a chance to consider between now and Monday.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I will call the resolution.

1. Resolved, That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Special War Revenue Act, 1915, and amending acts, by providing that the rate of the consumption or sales tax imposed by section nineteen BBB of the said act shall be reduced from six per cent to five per cent.

Mr. Chairman, I want to draw the attention of the House to the answer given at page 1834 of Hansard in connection with the sales tax administration, and to point out that a large number of firms have not paid the tax. The total number of firms in arrears is stated to be 3,170. This is a tax which is supposed to be collected promptly, it is a tax which is a day-to-day charge on the business, it is something which in the ordinary nature of things ought not to be allowed to stand. In the same way as a concern pays its monthly rent and its monthly salaries, so it ought to pay its sales tax. And I believe the department want to have the tax so paid. I am not now attributing any improper motives to the department or slackness one way or the other. The act as we have it, I think, absolutely invites delays, invites difficulties, invites fraud and invites the troubles which the department now finds itself in.
I have gone over the act and noted its provisions so I could have in my own head just for a short time what the act really means.
I am quite sure that when the act was considered none of us took the trouble to understand it, not even its introducer, and I am going to make this statement now so that my hon. friend will have a chance to go over it with a view to seeing what can be done to clean up the absolute jungle that exists with the administration of the sales tax. In the first instance, the fundamental idea upon which the tax is based is that it shall be payable only upon completely finished manufactured goods-that was the new idea we had last year-that is to say, goods which are sold to the ultimate consumer and do not undergo any further process of manufacture. I do not think I am wrong in starting out upon that basis. To carry out that idea different manufacturers are treated in different ways, and likewise different wholesalers are also treated in different ways. This is an offence right at the threshold against the ordinary first principles of taxation.
A manufacturer whose finished products are sold to be further manufactured gets his raw materials without the payment of the tax, and he can sell his products without the payment of the tax to another manufacturer or to a licensed wholesaler, but if he sells to an unlicensed wholesaler or retailer he has

Ways and Means-Sales Tax
to pay the tax. There, you see, you immediately have room for trouble; you have two different sets of accounting, and you have an immediate necessity for checking. Both these classes of manufacturers have to pay the tax on materials they buy in Canada or import which are not used in wrought into or attached to articles manufactured by them for sale. There is another subdivision. Under this provision all sorts of questions arise, and there are all kinds of different interpretations placed upon it by the manufacturers. A manufacturer who does not manufacture goods to the value of $10,000 per annum is not required to pay any sales tax on the goods he manufactures, but he has to pay the tax on materials he imports, and a licensed manufacturer or licensed wholesaler selling to such manufacturer has to pay the tax on such sales. But there is a qualification to this. Subsection 3 of section 6 of the act provides:
If the minister determines-
I pause, and am willing to wager anything that not a single member has been able to follow the effect of what I have said down to this point.
If the minister determines that any manufacturer or producer, who does not manufacture or produce goods to the value of ten thousand dollars a year, uses a substantial portion of goods which are exempt from the tax in the manufacture of goods which are liable to the tax, as to which the minister's finding shall be conclusive, such manufacturer or producer shall take out a license as required by subsection 6 of this section and shall be subject to the same conditions as a licensed manufacturer or producer.
Hon. gentlemen will see how perfectly clear this sub-section is, how easy to understand'! The one thing we can understand there is that that sub-section can be interpreted just according to the length of the minister's foot.
A clause in the act, subsection 9 of section 6-the reason for which it is difficult to understand except on the ground of protection
is that which declares that as respects goods which may be imported free of customs duty, the Minister of Customs is vested with power to grant a refund or deduction of the sales tax, not to exceed 25 per cent. That is to say, he can make the tax 4J per cent instead of 6 per cent on similar goods manufactured in Canada. It is made a condition of the exercise of this power that satisfactory evidence must be produced that such Canadian goods are at a disadvantage with respect to similar imported goods. I just pause to point out that apparently the idea of ministerial discretion in granting or withholding protection is pretty well carried out in the present budget

in connection with raw materials entering into the manufacture of so many articles that are now greatly reduced.
Dealing now with the wholesale trade, the act divides wholesalers into two categories- licensed and unlicensed. A licensed wholesaler is one 50 per cent or more of whose total sale of goods is to manufacturers, to be used, wrought into or attached to articles manufactured for sale, which, when sold, are subject to the sales tax. Unless a licensed wholesaler can come within that category, he is not entitled to a license even although the annual volume of his business may be as great, if not greater, than that of a wholesaler entitled to a license.
A licensed wholesaler can import or buy from a Canadian manufacturer, without the payment of the tax and sell without the payment of the tax to manufacturers, goods to be used in, wrought into or attached to articles to be manufactured for sale and subject to the tax when sold. Such licensed wholesaler has to pay the tax when he sells goods to persons, other than licensed manufacturers or licensed wholesalers. Plenty of room again for plenty of bookkeeping and plenty of mistakes.
An unlicensed wholesaler has to pay the tax on everything he imports, and licensed manufacturers or wholesalers selling to him have to pay the tax on their sales, which tax they will no doubt pass on to him.
If such unlicensed wholesaler should sell goods to a manufacturer to be used in, wrought into or attached to articles to be manufactured for sale and subject to the tax when sold, he is entitled to a refund of the tax paid upon making claim to the department, accompanied by proof of the payment of the tax and the sale and delivery to the manufacturer.
It is no exaggeration to state that at least 75 per cent of the wholesalers of the country would be treated as unlicensed wholesalers, and that consequently all the transactions of that large percentage of wholesale traders with manufacturers in respect of goods to be further manufactured, will be subject to refund in the Customs department involving tremendous private and official expense. It is no wonder that the return from the department is what it is.
Then again, subsection B of section 12a of the act provides that:
When goods are sold by a wholesaler or jobber not licensed under this act to a licensed manufacturer or producer, the purchaser shall be furnished with a written invoice of the goods sold, which invoice shall state separately the amount of the consumption o: sales tax.

Ways avd Means-Sales Tax
Compliance with this section clearly means a disclosure of the profit of the unlicensed wholesaler, because the tax which he paid and has to show in his invoice to the buyer from him was based on his-the unlicensed wholsaler's-purchase	price. Could anything be more absurd than to require a seller to disclose to his buyer the profit he is making on the transaction? The other licensed wholesaler has not to do that; but the unlicensed wholesaler, who has had to pay the tax and who is entitled to his refund, is put to the statutory disadvantage that he has to show plainly what his costs were.
In view of the provisions in the act for deduction, the act would be better entitled "The Sales Tax and Deduction Act." These deductions are as follows:
A manufacturer or a licensed wholesaler is entitled to a refund by way of deduction from sales tax returns, and the amount of the old sales tax paid directly to the government or to the person from whom he bought, on goods which he had on hand unsold on January 1, 1924, if such goods have been, are being or are to be .used in, wrought into or attached to articles to be manufactured or produced for sale and which are articles subject to the consumption or sales tax when sold.
To get this deduction each manufacturer and licensed wholesaler has to file an inventory of such goods and make claim therefor. The deduction is allowed to the manufacturer as he uses the goods-without reference to the sale thereof-and to the wholesaler when he sells the goods.
Under the language of the statute, a manufacturer could claim a deduction of the total amount of such tax without waiting to use up the goods upon which the tax was paid. Some manufacturers whose finished products are sold to enter into other manufactures, may not have any tax to pay, and, consequently, they are entitled to get back the tax paid on materials on hand on January 1, 1924, by way of refund after compiling inventories and making claims as above set forth.
Imagine, if you can, the tremendous amount of work to business firms with consequent expenses involved in compiling inventories and showing the tax paid thereon, in making claims for deduction and refund, and also the work to the officials of the Department of Customs in checking these inventories and claims. The plain, inescapable truth is that it will be almost impossible for the Customs department to make the proper necessary check of inventories. If there is any doubt about that, I think my hon. friend ought to look into the matter and see just how this
thing has worked out. A proper check would take years to make, and in the meantime business would be disorganized. It may be taken for granted that if any errors are made in preparing these inventories and claims, they will not be altogether in favour of the government. The door seems to be wide open to fraud on the revenue.
Unlicensed wholesalers get back by way of deduction or refund from sales tax returns, the tax paid upon materials they had on hand on January 1, and which they sell afterwards to manufacturers to be used in making articles subject to the tax. They must have had the materials on hand and a subsequent sale has to take place before this can be ascertained.
If a manufacturer making goods subject to the tax when sold should pay the tax on imported materials, he is entitled to get it back by way of deduction.
A refund of the tax may be granted on imported goods in respect to which customs duties have been refunded on exportation. This is a quotation-I will show it to the minister :
A deduction from the consumption or sales tax may be granted in respect to goods sold at a price fixed by a bona fide contract of sale made before the 12th day of May, 1923, and still in force at the time of delivery of the goods.
Section 13 of the act gives most extraordinary powers to the minister. It reads as follows:
Whenever goods are manufactured or produced in Canada under such circumstances or conditions as render it difficult to determine the value thereof for the consumption or sales tax because:
(a)	A lease of such goods or the right of using same but not the right' of property therein is sold or given; or
(b)	such goods having a royalty imposed thereon, the royalty is uncertain, or is not from other causes a reliable means of estimating the value of the goods; or,
(c)	such goods are manufactured by contract for labour only and not including the value of the goods that enter into the same, or under any other unusual or peculiar manner of conditions; or,
(d)	such goods are for use by the manufacturer or producer and not for sale.
Under this section it has been provided by regulation that:
In respect of goods subject to consumption or sales tax sold by retail by the manufacturer or producer thereof in Canada, the value of the goods for purposes of the tax will be determined by the Minister of Customs and Excise in each class of cases.
In other words, apart from the question of statutory rate, the minister has the absolute right to say what taxes shall be paid. It seems to me that any statute is absolutely indefensible which does not allow our business people to know what they have to pay when they operate; and no man in the world can

Ways and Means-Sales Tax
tell what he has to pay under this system. The minister can do what he pleases; no standard whatever is set up by which he is to be governed. Some manufacturers import goods which they might use in manufacturing other articles or may sell in the condition as imported. In such cases the manufacturers are entitled to import free of tax all such goods and they have to pay the tax when they sell such goods in the condition as imported based on the duty paid value of the goods when imported; which means going back to the customs entry and invoice. Here again there will be difficulty in checking returns. Every licensed manufacturer or licensed wholesaler buying goods in Canada to be used in making articles for sale subject to the tax, or which are for re-sale, has to quote his license number and give a certificate that the articles are to be used in making articles for sale, or are for re-sale; and he has to make similar license quotations and certificate on entries of imported goods. This of course means additional work to business firms and additional expense to the government in checking the returns to ensure that license numbers are quoted and certifications furnished in respect of non-taxable sales. Licensees are enjoined against quoting their license number and giving certificates as respects goods purchased by them consisting of plant, equipment or other goods for their own use and not for sale. A man has to be watching all the time to make sure that he is not infringing the regulations; he has to be on the qui vive to see that he is not breaking some provision of the act which renders him liable to penalty.	_
To-day there is absolutely no principle applied in connection with the administration of the act. It was attemped to be confined to the primary articles entirely, but that is something that has been lost sight of. There is no question of principle. For example, an application was made to the government-I am speaking from memory on the strength of a return I received-for exemptions in the cases of both newsprint and coffee. The sales tax on coffee was 6 per cent. What principle would determine the result that the sales tax on newsprint should be reduced 2^ per cent, which I think is the figure, while there should be no reduction of the sales tax on coffee? I am speaking of what is being done, and I hope that my hon. friend will take a note of the representations I am making in this regard. In connection with the collection of current taxes we have a muddled situation. I am not going to say for a single moment that there is anything dishonest about the matter. But just consider the answer which the minister gives to a question that is asked him:

In the balance of the cases the department is corresponding with the firms and individuals concerned with a view to making satisfactory arrangements for payment of arrears before legal action is taken.
These latter cases require nursing as drastic action would probably result in financial failures.
That is in connection with a tax that is coming due from day to day and which certainly ought to be settled monthly. We have such a mass and jungle of meaningless words in the act that it is impossible for one to carry it out intelligently. I want to give the Minister of Customs full credit both for industry and for intelligence, but he should not have to bring down a return like that. Surely to goodness the government having tried the freak legislation of last year ought to do something to put matters upon a more plain, if not a more logical, basis. At all events, let us pass legislation which will enable the people to know where they stand.

It is now approaching ten
o'clock and after we have adopted this resolution we shall adjourn. Before we do so however I want to acknowledge the statement which my hon. friend has placed on Hansard and to which I shall direct the attention of my colleague who is administering the act in question. I am prepared to agree with my hon. friend that there is difficulty in administering an act of this character. The fact is that no tax is popular, and if we could conceive of a tax that would meet with popular approval a large part of our troubles would disappear. I am sure that the hon. member, who was at one time head of the Finance department and responsible for collecting the revenue, must have had advice, as others in the department have had from time to time, as to the best methods of imposing taxation. I am not sure whether he was advised, as I have been, 10 p.m. that a popular and simple tax would be a turnover tax. There are those who say that we should have a tax on daily bank balances, while others advocate a land tax and others again a tax on bachelors. Well, I may say that some amendments as we come to them will in part at least remedy the difficulties that my hon. friend has pointed out. Regarding that part of the answer brought down to which my hon. friend has referred, concerning the "nursing" of certain businesses, I might observe that I am nursing along to-day, and am compelled as Acting Minister of Finance to nurse along, some institutions that are in arrears in taxes for which they were liable in the years when my hon. friend was Minister of Finance; and any unduly harsh treatment would put them out of business throwing many men out of employment. Taking all

Lausanne Treaty-Papers
tilings into consideration I think the taxes have been fairly well paid, and the people of Canada have responded fairly well to the demand for increased taxation to meet our war and other obligations. I shall direct the attention of my colleague to the observations of my hon. friend. It is the desire of the government as far as possible to simplify the collection of the sales tax, and we hope that the measures now submitted will have that effect. I trust the committee will pass the resolution.
Does the minister think that he should ask us to pass it to-night?

The present resolution only
involves the reducing of the tax on the various items from 6 to 5 per cent.

But the whole
principle is involved.
I do not press it.

On the question of nursing accounts, my hon. friend may have had a little sapling to work with but he has developed it into a whole forest. He says he has some legacies from me. I remember the time-I will not say my hon. friend did it; he had too much sense and honesty to do it

when any number of his associates were calling down vengeance from high heaven on my head because I did not put the Riordon Company out of business-just one concern.
Well, I never did.

I give my hon. friend credit for that; I say he had too much honesty and common sense to do it. But it was done and done all over, done at a time when their product was selling at a fraction of what it is bringing to-day. My hon. friends have done nothing with that account, have not collected five cents of it. Yes, it was in arrears with me something like three months after it came to my knowledge; my friends have been in office two years and nine months or thereabouts, but nothing is done. And it goes on growing. There is some difficulty in arriving at excess business profits where you have to follow everything and go through a whole arbitration before you can find it out, but there ought to be no difficulty in collecting current taxes; there ought to be no nursing of monthly accounts. That is the business my hon. friend's legislation would put him into.
Resolutions reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Robb thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. .127, to amend the Customs Tariff Act, 1907.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.
On motion of Mr. Robb the House adjourned at 10.07 p.m.
Monday, May 26, 1924
